raw_source: STATEMENT: A quantum circuit simulator is classical software that calculates what a quantum circuit does; it runs on classical hardware.
ground_truth.statement: A quantum circuit simulator is classical software that calculates what a quantum circuit does; it runs on classical hardware.

raw_source: STATEMENT: A general n-qubit pure state is described by 2ⁿ complex amplitudes; a state-vector simulator stores all of them.
ground_truth.statement: A general n-qubit pure state is described by 2ⁿ complex amplitudes; a state-vector simulator stores all of them.

raw_source: STATEMENT: At 16 bytes per amplitude (double-precision complex), the state-vector memory is 2ⁿ × 16 bytes: n = 20 → 16 MiB; n = 30 → 16 GiB; n = 40 → 16 TiB; n = 50 → 16 PiB.
VERIFICATION: Hand arithmetic (E01); confirm with a script.
ground_truth.statement: At 16 bytes per amplitude (double-precision complex), the state-vector memory is 2ⁿ × 16 bytes: n = 20 → 16 MiB; n = 30 → 16 GiB; n = 40 → 16 TiB; n = 50 → 16 PiB.
ground_truth.verification: Hand arithmetic (E01); confirm with a script.

raw_source: INPUT: |00⟩ → H on q0 → CNOT (control q0, target q1)
VERIFICATION: Hand calculation (E02); confirm in simulator (note Qiskit prints qubit order reversed, but this result is symmetric).
TOLERANCE: Exact in an ideal state-vector simulation; sampled counts vary statistically.
ground_truth.input: |00⟩ → H on q0 → CNOT (control q0, target q1)
ground_truth.verification: Hand calculation (E02); confirm in simulator (note Qiskit prints qubit order reversed, but this result is symmetric).
ground_truth.tolerance: Exact in an ideal state-vector simulation; sampled counts vary statistically.

raw_source: INPUT: |00⟩ → CNOT (control q0, target q1) → H on q0
VERIFICATION: Hand calculation (A01 "try this"); confirm in simulator.
ground_truth.input: |00⟩ → CNOT (control q0, target q1) → H on q0
ground_truth.verification: Hand calculation (A01 "try this"); confirm in simulator.

raw_source: STATEMENT: For an outcome with probability p estimated from N independent shots, the standard error of the measured frequency is √(p(1−p)/N); for p = 0.5 it is 0.05 at N = 100, ≈ 0.0158 at N = 1,000 and 0.005 at N = 10,000.
ground_truth.statement: For an outcome with probability p estimated from N independent shots, the standard error of the measured frequency is √(p(1−p)/N); for p = 0.5 it is 0.05 at N = 100, ≈ 0.0158 at N = 1,000 and 0.005 at N = 10,000.

raw_source: STATEMENT: Real quantum hardware returns sampled measurement outcomes; the full state vector is not directly readable (recovering it requires state tomography, whose cost grows exponentially with the number of qubits).
ground_truth.statement: Real quantum hardware returns sampled measurement outcomes; the full state vector is not directly readable (recovering it requires state tomography, whose cost grows exponentially with the number of qubits).

raw_source: STATEMENT: Circuits using only Clifford gates (such as H, S, CNOT) on computational-basis inputs, with computational-basis measurements, can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer (Gottesman–Knill theorem). Adding a non-Clifford gate such as T removes this guarantee.
VERIFICATION: Published results (Gottesman 1998; Aaronson and Gottesman 2004).
ground_truth.statement: Circuits using only Clifford gates (such as H, S, CNOT) on computational-basis inputs, with computational-basis measurements, can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer (Gottesman–Knill theorem). Adding a non-Clifford gate such as T removes this guarantee.

raw_source: INPUT: n-qubit GHZ circuit: H on q0, then CNOT from q0 to q1, q1 to q2, …, q(n−2) to q(n−1)
EXPECTED OUTPUT: (|00…0⟩ + |11…1⟩)/√2; P(all zeros) = 0.5, P(all ones) = 0.5, all other outcomes 0
VERIFICATION: Hand derivation (extension of E02, one CNOT per added qubit); confirm in simulator for small n (e.g. n = 3, 4).
ground_truth.input: n-qubit GHZ circuit: H on q0, then CNOT from q0 to q1, q1 to q2, …, q(n−2) to q(n−1)
ground_truth.expected_output: (|00…0⟩ + |11…1⟩)/√2; P(all zeros) = 0.5, P(all ones) = 0.5, all other outcomes 0
ground_truth.verification: Hand derivation (extension of E02, one CNOT per added qubit); confirm in simulator for small n (e.g. n = 3, 4).

raw_source: STATEMENT: Classical computers can in principle simulate any quantum circuit; the cost grows exponentially with qubit number in general, so quantum computers are expected to offer efficiency gains for some problems, not to compute classically uncomputable functions.

VERIFICATION: Standard result; whether quantum computers are strictly more efficient for all claimed tasks is an open theoretical question, so the tutor should say "expected" or "believed", not "proven".
ground_truth.statement: Classical computers can in principle simulate any quantum circuit; the cost grows exponentially with qubit number in general, so quantum computers are expected to offer efficiency gains for some problems, not to compute classically uncomputable functions.
ground_truth.verification: Standard result; whether quantum computers are strictly more efficient for all claimed tasks is an open theoretical question, so the tutor should say "expected" or "believed", not "proven".

raw_source: STATEMENT: Density-matrix simulation stores a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ matrix (memory ∝ 4ⁿ) and can represent noisy (mixed) states; state-vector simulation can represent noise only by randomly sampling error events across many runs.
ground_truth.statement: Density-matrix simulation stores a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ matrix (memory ∝ 4ⁿ) and can represent noisy (mixed) states; state-vector simulation can represent noise only by randomly sampling error events across many runs.

raw_source: STATEMENT: Project convention — the ideal state-vector simulator is the authoritative reference for what an ideal circuit does; it is not an authority on what a particular physical device will output.
VERIFICATION: Design decision, not a scientific fact.
